transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
U.S. Representative Hakeem Jeffries is on track to becoming the first black lawmaker
to serve as Speaker of the House.
Democrats have voted 251 to 11 to nominate him for a final vote on the House floor when
the new Congress convenes in January.
In a news conference a short time ago, Jeffries pledged the incoming Democratic majority
would deliver on their mandate to root out corruption and bring economic relief to the
American public.
We know the American people are struggling.
We know millions of people are drowning in this failed Republican economy, and House
Democrats are committed to turning things around.
With House Democrats securing the largest majority so far of the 21st century, Jeffries
can afford about 40 defections and still be elected Speaker, but he would also have to
work to unite factions, including Democrats elected in more than 50 districts President
Trump won in 2024.
A slew of recent digital service disruptions affecting everything from Microsoft Outlook
to flight communications are wreaking havoc across the Internet, but experts tell NPR's
Jenna McLaughlin there's no evidence cyber attacks are to blame.
The National Security Agency financial executives and others have told Congress that a series
of recent service outages affecting the NSA's classified networks, banking applications
and other digital services are the result of technical glitches caused by a large volume
of critical updates to systems.
That's according to a congressional source not authorized to speak on the record.
With the advent of artificial intelligence, it's becoming easier and faster to find vulnerabilities
in systems.
These are being forced to rapidly patch those holes to prevent attacks, but sometimes those
patches are difficult to apply or cause unintended disruptions.
Cybersecurity experts tell NPR the Internet has always been fragile and the industry is
still adjusting to the pace of updates in the age of AI.
Jenna McLaughlin, NPR News.
President Trump's Board of Peace is offering a sobering assessment of the conflict and
humanitarian crisis in Gaza, accusing both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments.
Here's NPR's Michelle Kellerman.
Israeli strikes continue in Gaza on a daily basis, despite the ceasefire established over
a year ago.
And Hamas has yet to meet its commitments.
Those are just some of the findings in the latest report by the Board of Peace.
It cites some improvement in access to food, but raises concerns about Israeli restrictions
on some basic needs ahead of winter, including shelter, sanitation and water.
Israel has not allowed candidates for a Gaza police force to go to Egypt for training,
and there's still no international stabilization force in place.
The report concludes that "the distance between what has been agreed and what is happening
on the ground remains the principal risk to the process."
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, the State Department.
It's NPR.
On the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, a White House official not authorized to speak
on the record confirms an expected meeting between President Trump and Russian President
Vladimir Putin, their first meeting since last year's Alaska Summit failed to end the
war in Ukraine.
This is expected before the trilateral summit between Trump, Putin and Chinese President
Xi Jinping.
Older adults are among the millions of people who've lost SNAP food aid in the past year.
That's after Republican lawmakers passed sweeping changes to the program.
NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports on what expanded work rules mean for one woman who retired
early.
Lisa Reese stopped working at 62 to help out family, including taking care of a granddaughter
to save on day care costs.
But she could barely get by as prices shot up this year, especially her gas bill.
Oh, my goodness.
That went through the roof.
One of my bills was $500.
This summer, she was approved for $63 a month in food aid.
And to get it under new work rules, she volunteers 80 hours a month at a local food pantry.
The Trump administration says such requirements are cutting costs and tackling fraud.
Reese loves helping out, but I have arthritis in my hand real bad, high blood pressure,
you name it.
She's not sure how long she can keep it up.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Capitol Heights, Maryland.
Well, after waiting 13 years, gamers worldwide are returning to Rockstar Games vice-shitty
with the rollout of Grand Theft Auto 6.
They can jump in at midnight local time Thursday.
This is NPR News.

Digital service outages, including Microsoft Outlook and flight communications, lack evidence of cyberattacks
Trump's Board of Peace report faults both Israel and Hamas for failing Gaza ceasefire commitments
White House confirms expected Trump-Putin meeting on sidelines of APEC Summit in China
Older adults losing SNAP food aid under expanded work rules, as one retiree volunteers at food pantry
Grand Theft Auto 6 launches worldwide, with gamers able to play from midnight Thursday
